title: Ringing Rocks County Park, Bucks County, Pennsylvania
seoTitle: Charter Bus to Ringing Rocks Park, Bucks County, PA
excerpt: A charter bus to Ringing Rocks County Park in Bucks County: bring hammers, mind the small parking lot, and know what the boulder field actually demands.

heroImage.alt: A field of large gray diabase boulders surrounded by woodland at Ringing Rocks County Park

extraImage.alt: A visitor striking a boulder with a hammer in the Ringing Rocks boulder field

body.text: A seven-acre field of gray boulders in the Bucks County woods that rings like struck metal when you hit it with a hammer. Not all of the rocks do, which is half the entertainment — a group spreads out across the field tapping stones and calling out when they find a live one. A charter bus to Ringing Rocks County Park makes an odd, genuinely memorable half-day out of what is otherwise a hard place to bring a group.
Bring hammers. Nobody supplies them.

This is the entire trip and it is remarkably easy to forget. A one to two pound ball-peen or club hammer per two or three people is right. Anything lighter does not produce the tone, and anything much heavier is tiring to carry across the field and harder on the rock.
Bring more than you think you need. The moment somebody finds a ringing boulder, everybody wants a turn, and a group of thirty sharing four hammers spends the visit queuing.
What the boulder field is actually like

It is a genuine boulder field, not a path through one. Getting into the middle means stepping and scrambling from rock to rock, with gaps and unstable footing. There is no route across it that is safe for anyone unsteady on their feet, and it is not accessible. Plan for part of the group to stay at the edge, where the rocks still ring and the walk in is level.

Solid closed shoes with grip, not sandals. Wet rock after rain is treacherous and the field has no shade in midsummer. A short trail also leads to High Falls, the tallest waterfall in Bucks County, which is a pleasant twenty minutes and often reduced to a trickle by August.
The parking lot decides which charter bus fits
The lot is small, unpaved and reached by narrow rural roads. This is not a park set up for coaches, and it is the constraint that shapes the booking more than the headcount does.

items: Twenty to thirty-two: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) is the sensible choice and the largest vehicle we would recommend without checking first.
Ten to fourteen: a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) parks without any difficulty and suits a scout troop, a geology club or a family group.

Forty to fifty-six: a full-size [charter bus](/fleet/motor-coaches) is workable only as a drop-off with the coach waiting elsewhere. Tell us in advance and we will arrange it rather than discovering the problem on the lane.

body.text: Getting there

The park is near Upper Black Eddy in northern Bucks County, close to the Delaware River. From [Doylestown](/locations/pennsylvania/doylestown) it is about half an hour, from [Quakertown](/locations/pennsylvania/quakertown) around twenty-five minutes, from [Easton](/locations/pennsylvania/easton) twenty, and from [Philadelphia](/locations/pennsylvania/philadelphia) roughly an hour and a quarter.

It is a two-hour stop, not a day, so build something around it. The river towns of New Hope and Frenchtown are both close and make an easy afternoon. Groups searching for charter bus rental near me in Bucks County usually get better value asking for a half-day itinerary than a single transfer, because the region rewards moving between several small places.
Why the rocks ring, as far as anyone knows

The boulders are diabase, a dense volcanic rock, and the field is a relic of freeze-thaw weathering at the end of the last ice age. Why some of them ring and others do not is still not fully settled. The leading explanation is internal stress within the rock combined with the way individual boulders sit — a stone resting on others rings, while the same stone half-buried in soil thuds.

Tests have shown that a ringing rock removed from the field stops ringing, which is the detail that most reliably fascinates a school group. It also happens to be a useful argument for leaving them where they are.

For a science class this is a genuinely good site: an observable phenomenon with a partial explanation and a real open question, which is a rarer thing on a field trip than it should be. Our [school trip transportation](/services/school-trips) team handles a steady number of these each spring.
When to go

Spring and autumn are best: cool enough for the exposed field, and the waterfall actually runs. Summer visits should start early, because the boulders sit in full sun and hold the heat. Winter is workable on a dry day but ice on the rocks makes the field genuinely dangerous, and it is not a trip to run with a group in those conditions.
